Feminines in -υς that lengthen the υ are accented with an acute: πληθύς, ἐδητύς, ὀϊζύς, ἐρινύς, ἰξύς ‘the spine’, ἰσχύς, ἰλύς, κλιτύς, ἀλητύς, ῥυστακύς, ἀγλύς—remarkable in its inflection; for it is declined with -θος, not with a pure -ος. But νηδύς, by poetic license, is shortened, as in Callimachus (h. Dian. 160) “ἔτι οἱ πάρα νηδὺς ἐκείνη” and in Euripides in the Andromache (356) “καὶ νηδὺν ἐξαμβλοῦμεν ὡς αὐτὸς λέγει”. Noted among the feminines are ὀφρῦς and ὀσφῦς ‘the spine’, with circumflex. Diminutives in -υς take a circumflex: καμμῦς, κλαυσῦς, λαρδῦς, Διονῦς, ἀπφῦς. original.english_translation: It was called Ταφίων. Εὐβοΐς, Τρωΐς, Ἀθωΐς, Ὁμολωΐς: the Ὁμολωΐδες are gates of Thebes by the mountain. Ἀχελωΐς. But the discussion concerns Greek names, lest someone cite Ξόϊς and Σάϊς, which are Egyptian and are mentioned in Herodotus. Likewise also Θμοῦις, a city of Egypt, and Σύϊς, a city of Egypt, as Hecataeus says in his Periegesis, and Κρῶϊς, a city of the Arabs, are accented with the grave. By this principle δαΐς “battle” is also accented with the acute, unless someone should say that this is given a grave accent by way of contrast with the form accented with the acute, just as ἀκρίς too. But Κράταιϊς seems, in the proper name, to be given a grave accent because of the accusative “βωστρεῖν δὲ Κράταιϊν” (Od. μ 124); yet perhaps this too is by way of distinction. And νηΐς, only in the feminine, in the sense of the nymph, is accented with the acute; but νῆϊς, the masculine, meaning “inexperienced,” as in “νῆϊς ἀέθλων,” is accented with the grave. Words ending in -ις that are barytone are barytone also in composition: μῆτις πολύμητις, ἴδρις ἄϊδρις, πόλις φιλόπολις, χάρις εὔχαρις. Feminines ending in -ις that are oxytone—if in composition they preserve only the feminine gender, they preserve the same accent; but if they become transferable and also masculine, they necessarily shift also to a grave accent. Of the former type, preserving the same gender and the same accent: σκελίς περισκελίς, νυχίς παννυχίς; of the latter: ἐλπίς δύσελπις. Accordingly καταιγίς is accented with the acute, but μελάναιγις with the grave. Thus then εὐκλήϊς and πολυκλήϊς and μελαμψήφις will also be accented with the grave; for they are used also of the masculine, just as, conversely, λεύκασπις. For it could be applied also to an Amazon. And εὐκνήμις likewise is in fact applied to Athena by Rhianus in the Thessalica: “τοὶ δ´ ἤδη ἐπὶ νηὸν ἐϋκνήμιδος Ἰτώνης.” Derivatives in -ις are accented with the acute: δρυμός Δρυμίς (“Δρυμίδες νύμφαι”), λόγος (“Λογίδες σεμναί”), φορμός (“φορμίς: a little dried fig”) in Alexis. Κάδμος Καδμίς in Ibycus: “παρελέξατο Καδμίδι κούρᾳ”; Παρνασσός Παρνασσίς, Μολοσσός Μολοσσίς, Κηφισός Κηφισίς.

Read the qualifications

Compounds with shortened υ are proparoxytone: an acute on the antepenult. Feminines with lengthened υ are oxytone: an acute on the last syllable. The cited diminutives have a circumflex.

A circumflex alone does not establish a diminutive: the passage excepts ὀσφῦς, ὀφρῦς and ἰχθῦς from that inference. It explicitly concludes that ἰξύς is oxytone despite the earlier classification it discusses.

νηδύς can have shortened υ by poetic licence: Callimachus (h. Dian. 160) and Euripides, Andromache (356). These examples illustrate this passage, not a complete Greek accent engine.

Play with a rule from Περὶ καθολικῆς προσῳδίας 1.85: how some Greek words in -ις keep or shift their accent in compounds.

1) Look up a cited base in -ις

Enter a cited Greek word ending in ις (e.g. μῆτις, χάρις, ἐλπίς, καταιγίς). Accents may be included or omitted. In derivative mode, enter the cited noun in -ος and leave the prefix blank. Only attested combinations listed here are returned.

Choose the passage’s scenario

Normalized (no accents)

What changed?
—
Scope and accent terminology

This explorer returns the passage’s cited forms, preserving their spellings, rather than generating new compounds. Barytone here means accent not on the last syllable; it does not require a written grave accent or an accent on the penult. For example, μῆτις → πολύμητις and ἐλπίς → δύσελπις.

Prefix joining is not always simple concatenation: νυχίς → παννυχίς and καταιγίς → μελάναιγις are displayed exactly as cited. Other combinations receive no generated accent.

Based on Aelius Herodianus 1.85 (on -ις words, compounds, and accent behavior).

original.english_translation: It was called Ταφίων. Εὐβοΐς, Τρωΐς, Ἀθωΐς, Ὁμολωΐς: the Ὁμολωΐδες are gates of Thebes by the mountain. Ἀχελωΐς. But the discussion concerns Greek names, lest someone cite Ξόϊς and Σάϊς, which are Egyptian and are mentioned in Herodotus. Likewise also Θμοῦις, a city of Egypt, and Σύϊς, a city of Egypt, as Hecataeus says in his Periegesis, and Κρῶϊς, a city of the Arabs, are accented with the grave. By this principle δαΐς “battle” is also accented with the acute, unless someone should say that this is given a grave accent by way of contrast with the form accented with the acute, just as ἀκρίς too. But Κράταιϊς seems, in the proper name, to be given a grave accent because of the accusative “βωστρεῖν δὲ Κράταιϊν” (Od. μ 124); yet perhaps this too is by way of distinction. And νηΐς, only in the feminine, in the sense of the nymph, is accented with the acute; but νῆϊς, the masculine, meaning “inexperienced,” as in “νῆϊς ἀέθλων,” is accented with the grave. Words ending in -ις that are barytone are barytone also in composition: μῆτις πολύμητις, ἴδρις ἄϊδρις, πόλις φιλόπολις, χάρις εὔχαρις. Feminines ending in -ις that are oxytone—if in composition they preserve only the feminine gender, they preserve the same accent; but if they become transferable and also masculine, they necessarily shift also to a grave accent. Of the former type, preserving the same gender and the same accent: σκελίς περισκελίς, νυχίς παννυχίς; of the latter: ἐλπίς δύσελπις. Accordingly καταιγίς is accented with the acute, but μελάναιγις with the grave. Thus then εὐκλήϊς and πολυκλήϊς and μελαμψήφις will also be accented with the grave; for they are used also of the masculine, just as, conversely, λεύκασπις. For it could be applied also to an Amazon. And εὐκνήμις likewise is in fact applied to Athena by Rhianus in the Thessalica: “τοὶ δ´ ἤδη ἐπὶ νηὸν ἐϋκνήμιδος Ἰτώνης.” Derivatives in -ις are accented with the acute: δρυμός Δρυμίς (“Δρυμίδες νύμφαι”), λόγος (“Λογίδες σεμναί”), φορμός (“φορμίς: a little dried fig”) in Alexis. Κάδμος Καδμίς in Ibycus: “παρελέξατο Καδμίδι κούρᾳ”; Παρνασσός Παρνασσίς, Μολοσσός Μολοσσίς, Κηφισός Κηφισίς.

Notes (what this is and isn’t)
  • This is a toy: it doesn’t fully compute Greek accentuation. It demonstrates the idea in Herodian: some -ις words keep their accent in compounds; some shift when the compound becomes “transferable” to masculine.
  • Accents are placed with a simple rule: oxytone = acute on the last vowel; barytone = acute on the penult vowel (when possible).
  • For “paronymic” -ις, the gadget replaces final -ος with -ίς and accents the last syllable.

Based on Aelius Herodianus 1.85 (on -ις words, compounds, and accent behavior).
